fixes.explanation: Glad is exactly the word. David says, “I was glad when they said to me…” and then he gives the invitation: “Let us go to the house of the LORD.” Nobody had to drag him there. I think that's the kind of gladness you can see from across the room, like a baker when the oven timer dings on a good batch.
Not afraid, friend. David says, “I was glad when they said to me…” The invitation made him happy, not nervous. Nothing in the verse says he was shaking in his sandals.
Not unsure at all. David says right out, “I was glad when they said to me…” You won't find a “let me check my calendar” anywhere in that line. Glad is the word he gives us.
Joppa isn't where David puts them. He says, “Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem.” The song is about arriving at the city. Put the sunscreen away, friend.
True. David says the tribes go up “…to give thanks to the name of the LORD.” That's the reason the song gives for the trip. They go to give thanks, and I think that's a good reason to travel.

Glory sounds shiny and right, but it's not the word here. David says, “For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David.” Judgment is the word the text gives. These are thrones of the house of David.

Wisdom is a lovely word, and I can see why it tempts you. But David says, “For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David.” Judgment is the word on those thrones. Wisdom will just have to sit this one out.
That's not what David says to pray for. His instruction is, “Pray for the peace of Jerusalem…” The song doesn't mention enemies falling at all. Peace is what he tells them to pray for.
True. The prayer goes, “May those who love you prosper.” Those words are for the ones who love Jerusalem. Me, I'd be standing there saying, “uh… good stuff… amen.”
Hold up, that one's TRUE, friend! The prayer David gives says, “May those who love you prosper.” Those who love Jerusalem are right there in the words. No tricks, and I checked it twice.

His brothers and friends, that's the reason he gives. David says, “For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say…” and the words he'll say are “Peace be within you.” It's all for them. I bet that lands warmer than any “talk to you later.”

The song never says that. David gives his reason himself: “For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say…” His brothers and friends are the reason, not the crowds. I think a friend's blessing beats applause any day.
No elders show up in this song. David says, “For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say…” The reason is his brothers and friends. Nobody handed him a clipboard and an assignment.

House is the word. David ends with, “For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity.” The song began with the house of the LORD in verse 1 and finishes there too. That's like walking a loop around the block and ending up back at your own front door.
